title: Trending — Predictors and prevalence of support for white nationalism in the United States
one_line: Three national surveys of non-Hispanic white US adults (2021–2025) used a direct, information-first question — describing white nationalist tenets then asking for support — to estimate prevalence and test strain, status-threat and online-mobilisation accounts.
key_claims: In the NORC AmeriSpeak probability sample (n=2,114, 2024), 4.9% of non-Hispanic white adults endorsed support (CI 3.6–6.2), rising to 13.5% among white men aged 18–29 (CI 6.0–21.0).

Status threat found no support: county racial diversity and recent change in white share were non-significant (P<0.08, opposite-signed) with equivalence tests passed; rural/urban null (delta-BIC ~21).
Strain predictors held: three or more personal hardships in past year +4 points, top-vs-bottom county social distress +4 points; occupational decline null but equivalence test failed.

Online-only friendship, not social media use, tracked support: all three closest friends known only online was +13 points, while frequency of use (delta-BIC ~8) and political social media activity (delta-BIC ~23) were null.

The measure looks distinct from existing scales: r=0.40 white identity, 0.31 great replacement, 0.26 old-fashioned racism, 0.25 racial resentment, 0.15 white privilege denial; informing respondents raised endorsement 3.8%→7.6% in study one (n=3,227, P<0.001) but not in study two (3.0% vs 4.3%, P=0.25).

Other correlates: education 15-point spread, income 7, religious attendance +4, conservatives +8, Republicans +5, Trump-2020 voters +6, government conspiracy thinking +9; all survive multivariate except income.
limitations: Reverse-keyed wording ('Are you an opponent?') produced endorsement 9 points higher (P<0.001), an unexplained gap; after acquiescence adjustment, age-among-men (P=0.16) and education (P=0.15) fall below conventional significance.
Authors state expressed support is not organisational affiliation, which was not measured.
Cross-sectional data: authors note the online-friendship arrow could run the other way, and theory tests are labelled corroborative, not causal.
NORC cumulative response rate was 2.7% with non-responses counted as 'no'; the claim that non-response biases the estimate downward is an argument, not a measurement.

Study one is a matched opt-in panel resting on the unverifiable assumption that participation is independent of the stigmatised attitudes measured; sensitivity analysis flags county social distress as most vulnerable to omitted-variable bias.
The 13.5% young-men interval is 15 points wide; the 2.5-point equivalence threshold was pre-set but not preregistered.
open_questions: Field the same item to the same panel years apart to separate cohort from life-cycle effects in the young-white-men result.
Explain the 9-point reverse-keying gap before treating 4.9% as a wording-independent prevalence.
Resolve whether the information treatment has a real effect, given study one's doubling and study two's failed-equivalence null.
Longitudinal or design-based evidence on whether online-only friendship precedes or follows these attitudes.
